snip.t: CT/MR angiography: Is there aortic coarctation or aneurysm? — Narrowing of aortic arch, delayed femoral pulses

Safety: Anticoagulation is generally contraindicated or held in active native-valve infective endocarditis due to the high risk of fatal intracerebral haemorrhage from septic embolic infarctions or ruptured mycotic aneurysms.

Vasculitis is a heterogeneous group of disorders characterised by inflammation of blood vessel walls, leading to vessel wall damage, luminal narrowing or occlusion, aneurysm formation and downstream tissue ischaemia or necrosis.

Understanding that inflammation can begin in any layer but most clinically relevant damage occurs when the media and adventitia are breached, causing aneurysm or rupture, or when the intima thickens, causing stenosis.
Left ventricular aneurysm formation causing persistent ST-segment elevation, chronic heart failure, and systemic thromboembolism.

qs.q: A 50-year-old man with septic shock secondary to a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm remains hypotensive despite initial balanced crystalloid resuscitation and correction of his surgical bleeding source. According to ICU management guidelines, what is the first-line vasoactive agent of choice to restore perfusion pressure?
qs.e: Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor of choice in septic and vasodilatory shock when fluid resuscitation fails to restore adequate mean arterial pressure. Dobutamine is reserved as an inotrope if myocardial dysfunction is present.
qs.s: Surgical Critical Care: ICU, Respiratory Failure, Ventilation, Blood: MCQs

qs.q: A 72-year-old man undergoes an open repair of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm within two hours of presentation. How is this operation classified according to its surgical urgency?
qs.e: Emergency operations are indicated immediately within hours for life-threatening conditions such as a ruptured aneurysm or bowel perforation. Urgent procedures are typically performed within days for conditions like an obstructed bowel.
qs.s: Pre-operative Management: Assessment, Risk Scoring and Optimisation: MCQs

qs.q: A 52-year-old man collapses after a sudden severe headache. A non-contrast CT head performed 4 hours later demonstrates high attenuation within the basal cisterns and subarachnoid spaces. Which anatomical site is the most frequent location for the underlying ruptured aneurysm?
o: Internal carotid artery and posterior communicating junction
qs.e: About 85% of saccular aneurysms occur in the anterior circulation, with the internal carotid artery including the posterior communicating junction being the most common site at 41%. The anterior communicating artery is the second most common site at 34%.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and smoking is found to have an unruptured saccular aneurysm. Which of the following inherited systemic conditions is strongly associated with the development of intracranial berry aneurysms?
qs.e: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is a well-known risk factor for intracranial saccular aneurysms, alongside other conditions like coarctation of the aorta and Marfan syndrome. Huntington disease and neurofibromatosis do not share this specific vascular association.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

qs.q: A 50-year-old female presents with a severe thunderclap headache and is found to have a complete left-sided third cranial nerve palsy, including a dilated, unreactive pupil and ptosis, along with retro-orbital pain. Which specific aneurysm site is most consistent with this localising sign?
qs.e: An aneurysm at the internal carotid or posterior communicating artery can cause compression of the third cranial nerve, leading to ipsilateral ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, and a dilated pupil. Other locations present with different focal deficits such as aphasia or bilateral leg weakness.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

qs.q: A 42-year-old woman with a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm presents with confusion, bilateral leg weakness, and urinary incontinence alongside abulia and personality changes. Which arterial territory is directly implicated in causing these specific localising signs?
qs.e: Anterior communicating artery aneurysms can affect the anterior cerebral artery territory, resulting in bilateral leg weakness, abulia, and personality changes due to involvement of the frontal lobes. Middle cerebral artery aneurysms typically cause contralateral face or hand weakness and aphasia.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

qs.q: What primary pathophysiologic mechanism explains the formation of saccular aneurysms at arterial branch points in the circle of Willis?
o: Defect of tunica media and internal elastic lamina combined with hemodynamic stress
Autoimmune vasculitis causing endothelial basement membrane damage and perivascular inflammation
Atherosclerotic plaque rupture leading to localized arterial thrombosis and vessel remodeling
Infectious destruction of the arterial wall by septic emboli with subsequent inflammation
qs.e: Saccular aneurysms develop where a congenital or acquired defect in the media and elastic lamina is exposed to high hemodynamic stress at arterial bifurcations. Atherosclerotic plaque rupture, infection, and vasculitis cause different vascular lesions.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

qs.q: A 54-year-old woman is admitted to the neurosurgical intensive care unit following a ruptured cerebral aneurysm. Her mean arterial pressure is 145 mmHg and systolic blood pressure is 175 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent to initiate for acute blood pressure control?
qs.e: Labetalol is a titratable agent with a short half-life that controls blood pressure without increasing intracranial pressure. Nitrates should be avoided because they raise intracranial pressure.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

es.q: Describe the methods used to secure intracranial aneurysms and prevent rebleeding.
es.m:
- **Timing of intervention:** Aneurysms must be secured early (within 24 to 72 hours) because rebleeding risk peaks strongly in the first 24 hours and accounts for high mortality.
- **Surgical clipping:** Involves a craniotomy to place a titanium clip across the aneurysm neck; highly recommended for Hunt and Hess grades 1 to 3.
- **Indications for clipping:** Particularly favoured for middle cerebral artery aneurysms, large or wide-necked aneurysms, presence of haematoma, and when the dome gives off branches.
- **Endovascular coiling:** A catheter is passed from the femoral artery into the aneurysm to pack platinum coils into the sac, inducing thrombosis.

ai.title: Aneurysm
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: An aneurysm is a focal dilatation of a blood vessel wall due to structural weakness. In low‑resource settings the most common causes are infectious (tuberculous, syphilitic, mycotic) and inflammatory (vasculitis, rheumatic disease).

sections.p: An aneurysm is a localized, permanent dilation of a vessel exceeding 50% of its normal diameter. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion and imaging; when CT/MRI are unavailable, bedside ultrasound or plain radiographs can suggest a large mass or pulsatile swelling.

t.b: Is there a pulsatile, anechoic cavity? – Aaneurysm appears as a saccular or fusiform echo‑free space with blood flow on Doppler.
Does a soft‑tissue mass have a calcified rim? – Calcification suggests chronic aneurysm; absence does not rule out acute disease.

sections.p: Aneurysms are staged by size, growth rate and risk of rupture. The Society for Vascular Surgery (SVS) grading classifies abdominal aortic aneurysms: I (<5.5 cm), II (5.5–6.5 cm), III (>6.5 cm).
b: Size >5.5 cm or rapid growth >0.5 cm/year

sections.p: In East Africa the leading causes are infectious and inflammatory. The table lists common etiologies in order of likelihood.
b: Infectious: TB, syphilis, HIV‑associated mycotic aneurysm
Inflammatory: Takayasu arteritis, Kawasaki disease, rheumatic heart disease

sections.p: Presentation depends on location. Common features include a pulsatile mass, localized pain, and systemic signs of infection or inflammation.
When advanced imaging is unavailable, use the most accessible tests to rule out rupture and assess size.

t.b: Is the vessel dilated and does it have a thrombus? – Confirms aneurysm and shows intraluminal clot.
Is there leukocytosis or anemia? – Suggests infection or chronic blood loss.
Is inflammation elevated? – Supports vasculitis or infectious etiology.
Are there positive antibodies? – Identifies specific infectious causes.
Is there a calcified rim? – Indicates chronic aneurysm.

sections.p: Urgent care is required if there are signs of rupture or impending rupture.
Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care. Anticoagulation is avoided if infection is present.
b: Penicillin for syphilitic aneurysm (penicillin G 3–4 million IU q4h for 10–14 days)
Surgical repair or endovascular stent graft if size >5.5 cm or symptomatic

sections.p: Regular imaging every 6–12 months for stable aneurysms; control blood pressure, treat infections, and counsel on smoking cessation.
Aneurysm can be mistaken for a tumour, abscess or hematoma.
b: Abscess – usually tender, fluctuating, no pulsation

sections.p: Low‑grade infection may give normal CRP; small aneurysms may be missed on plain X‑ray.
Any sudden change in pain, haemodynamic instability or neurological deficit warrants immediate transfer.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of aortic aneurysm in East Africa?

faq.a: Yes, many are found incidentally on imaging for other reasons.
Only if the aneurysm is >5.5 cm, symptomatic, or rapidly expanding; otherwise surveillance is acceptable.

exam: What is the first investigation you would order for a patient with a pulsatile abdominal mass in a low‑resource setting? — Bedside ultrasound to confirm aneurysm and assess thrombus.
How would you differentiate a mycotic aneurysm from atherosclerotic aneurysm clinically? — Fever, leukocytosis, positive infection serology versus isolated hypertension and smoking history.

A patient with a known abdominal aneurysm presents with sudden severe pain and hypotension. What is your immediate management? — Suspect rupture: stabilize haemodynamics, arrange emergency transfer, avoid anticoagulation.
Why is anticoagulation contraindicated in a mycotic aneurysm? — Risk of haemorrhage from infected vessel wall and septic emboli.
Which drug class is preferred for treating syphilitic aneurysm? — Penicillin G, high‑dose intravenous for 10–14 days.
In a patient with a 6.0 cm abdominal aneurysm and uncontrolled hypertension, what is the next best step? — Tight blood‑pressure control, schedule elective repair, and monitor size every 6 months.
